families.s: HSE control of hazardous substances in agriculture
families.t: dusts, pesticides, veterinary medicines, gases, biological agents, elimination, enclosure, ventilation, surveillance
f: COSHH covers hazardous substances used, generated or naturally occurring in agricultural work.
Examples include pesticides, veterinary medicines, disinfectants and fertilisers.
Generated hazards include welding fume, grain dust, poultry dust and slurry or silo gases.
Biological agents such as bacteria and fungi are also covered.
Exposure should first be eliminated where reasonably practicable.
Enclosure, extraction, filtered cabs and safer materials can reduce exposure.
RPE and skin protection may be needed for residual risk but should not replace source controls.
Health surveillance is normally needed for continuing exposure to grain dust or other sensitisers.

families.s: HSE prevention of zoonotic infection in agricultural work and farm visits
families.t: animals, micro-organisms, COSHH, hygiene, vulnerable visitors, E coli, cryptosporidium, information and control
f: Farm animals naturally carry diseases that can also affect humans.
Zoonoses are caused by micro-organisms and are subject to COSHH.
Employers should assess and prevent or adequately control exposure.
Control measures should be introduced, maintained and reviewed.
Workers need information, instruction and training about risks and precautions.
Visitors can also be exposed, especially children and older people.
E coli O157 and Cryptosporidium are examples of serious farm-associated infections.
Hygiene, animal-contact controls and suitable visitor arrangements are central preventive measures.

families.s: HSE control of poultry-dust respiratory exposure
families.t: bedding, bird handling, catching, litter, cleaning, bioaerosols, RPE, face fit and surveillance
f: Poultry dust contains feed, bedding, faecal material, feathers, dander, mites and micro-organisms.
Some components are allergens or asthmagens capable of causing occupational asthma.
Dust is generated during bedding, stocking, inspection, catching, litter removal and final cleaning.
Respirable particles can penetrate into the gas-exchange region of the lungs.
COSHH requires exposure to be prevented or adequately controlled.
Engineering controls, ventilation and good work practices should be used before relying on RPE.
Tight-fitting respirators require face-fit testing and correct use.
Workers exposed to asthmagens should receive suitable health surveillance and training.

families.s: HSE workplace safety, welfare, fire and confined-space controls on farms
families.t: yards, edges, obstructions, welfare, confined spaces, fire escape, alarms, extinguishers and diversification
f: Agricultural workplaces should control slips, trips, open edges and falls into tanks or pits.
Work areas should be clear of cables, sacks, pallets and other obstructions.
Adequate space, storage and welfare facilities should be provided.
Confined and poorly ventilated spaces require assessment and suitable precautions before entry.
Fire precautions should include clear escape routes and effective alarms.
Workers should know how to raise the alarm and use suitable extinguishers.
Fire alarms and extinguishers require regular checking and maintenance.
Farm diversification should reassess public, child, traffic and livestock-interaction risks.

families.s: HSE notification, marking and safe storage of dangerous substances and ammonium nitrate on farms
families.t: NAMOS, quantities, fire service, HSE notification, site marking, oxidisers, combustibles and records
f: NAMOS places notification and site-marking duties on farms storing specified quantities of dangerous substances.
Sites storing 25 tonnes or more of dangerous substances must notify the local Fire and Rescue Service.
The same threshold can require notification to HSE and warning signs at the entrance.
Relevant ammonium-nitrate mixtures are identified by nitrogen content and stored quantity.
Large quantities of relevant ammonium nitrate require Fire and Rescue Service notification.
Dutyholders should inventory products, hazard classifications and quantities before applying thresholds.
Ammonium nitrate is an oxidiser and should be separated from combustible materials.
Notifications, warning signs and safe-storage controls should be kept current when inventories change.
